name: Teufelberger treeMOTION CE Replacement Leg Strap Kit
title: Teufelberger treeMOTION Replacement Leg Strap Kit
h1: Teufelberger treeMOTION Replacement Leg Strap Kit (CE)
meta: A treeMOTION replacement leg strap kit for the CE version of Teufelberger's saddle. What it replaces, when to retire worn leg loops, and how to check the fit.
tagline: Factory leg loops for the CE treeMOTION, to keep a good saddle working.
summary: This treeMOTION replacement leg strap kit supplies new leg loops for the CE version of Teufelberger's climbing saddle. Leg loops take a beating from spurs, sap, and grit, and swapping them is often cheaper than retiring a saddle whose bridge, board, and waist belt are still in good shape.
highlights: Factory replacement leg loops for the CE treeMOTION
Restores fit and comfort on a worn saddle
Cheaper than replacing the whole saddle
Install per Teufelberger's instructions
Inspect the rest of the saddle at the same time

body.h: Why replace leg straps instead of the saddle
p: On a treeMOTION the leg loops see more wear than almost any other part. They rub on spur straps, take every sit-back in the work position, and pick up pitch and sand that grind at the webbing and padding. Once they are frayed, stiff, or flattened out, the saddle starts to feel wrong long before the bridge or the waist belt is done.

A factory leg strap kit lets you bring the saddle back to spec without buying a new one. Check that you have the CE version of the treeMOTION before you order; Teufelberger has made several generations, and parts are not always interchangeable. Other wear parts are in our saddle parts and shoulder harnesses section.

Follow Teufelberger's instructions for removing the old loops and installing the new ones, and have a competent person check the work if you are unsure. Life-support gear has to be assembled exactly as the maker intended and must meet ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's requirements.

While the saddle is apart, inspect everything else: the bridge, the connecting hardware, the waist belt stitching, and the attachment points. Look for cuts, abrasion, glazing, chemical stains, and worn or distorted metal. Replace anything questionable, and keep a record of the date and what was changed.

faq.q: Will these leg straps fit a treeMOTION evo or S.LIM?
faq.a: Do not assume so. This kit is listed for the CE treeMOTION. Confirm your saddle model and check Teufelberger's parts guidance before ordering.

faq.q: When should treeMOTION leg straps be replaced?
faq.a: Replace them when you see cuts, fraying, glazing, crushed padding, damaged stitching, or anything that fails the manufacturer's inspection criteria.

name: Teufelberger treeMOTION evo Replacement Back Pad
title: Teufelberger treeMOTION evo Back Pad Replacement
meta: A treeMOTION evo back pad to replace a worn or crushed one. How the pad affects comfort on long climbs, fitting tips, and what to inspect on the saddle.
tagline: A fresh back pad for the treeMOTION evo, for climbers who spend all day in the saddle.
summary: The treeMOTION evo back pad is the padded section that carries your lower back in the work position on Teufelberger's evo saddle. After a few seasons the padding packs down and the cover wears through, and a new pad brings back the support that made the saddle comfortable.
highlights: Replacement back pad for the treeMOTION evo
Restores support for long hangs in the work position
Swap a worn pad instead of the whole saddle
Good time to inspect the rest of the saddle
specs: Comfort part for tree climbing saddle

body.h: What a worn back pad costs you
p: A flattened back pad does not usually make a saddle unsafe, but it makes long days harder. You sit back to make a cut, the pad no longer spreads the load, and pressure shifts to the waist belt edges and your hips. Over a week of pruning or a big removal, that adds up to sore backs and shorter climbs.

Replacing the pad is a straightforward way to keep a good evo in service. Make sure it is the evo version; earlier treeMOTION models used different pads. For leg straps, bridges, and other wear items, see our saddle parts.

Climbers who spend long hours in the work position, such as on big pruning jobs or crane removals where you wait on picks, notice the difference most. A fresh pad brings back the support the saddle had when it was new.

Install the pad following Teufelberger's instructions so that nothing load-bearing is rerouted or left twisted. If the pad's attachment touches any part of the life-support system, have a competent person confirm the saddle is correctly assembled before you climb on it.

Use the swap as a full inspection. Check the bridge and rings, the stitching at every load point, the side D-rings, and the buckles. Retire any saddle or component that shows cuts, heat damage, chemical contact, or excessive wear, as ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer require.

faq.q: Does the evo back pad fit the original treeMOTION?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Teufelberger changed the design between models, so match the pad to the evo or check the maker's parts list.

faq.q: Is the back pad a load-bearing part?
faq.a: Treat it as part of the saddle and install it exactly as Teufelberger specifies. Inspect the load-bearing parts of the saddle whenever you change it.

name: Weaver Cougar Replacement Webbing Bridge
title: Weaver Cougar Replacement Webbing Bridge
meta: A Weaver Cougar replacement webbing bridge for the Cougar climbing saddle. Why bridges wear first, how to fit one correctly, and when to retire it for good.
tagline: A replacement webbing bridge for the Weaver Cougar saddle.
summary: This Weaver Cougar replacement webbing bridge replaces the bridge on Weaver's Cougar climbing saddle. The bridge carries your climbing system and rubs against hardware all day, so it is usually the first part of a saddle to need replacing.
highlights: Replacement bridge for the Weaver Cougar saddle
Webbing construction
Bridges wear fastest, so plan to replace them
Inspect before every climb

body.h: Why the bridge wears out first
p: Your hitch, friction device, or ring slides along the bridge every time you move around the tree. That constant traffic, plus sap and grit, wears webbing faster than any other part of the saddle. On a saddle you use every day, a bridge can need replacing well before the rest of it.

Keeping a spare Weaver Cougar bridge in the truck means a worn one does not have to end your day or your saddle. Make sure it is the right part for your Cougar model. More spares are in our saddle parts and shoulder harnesses section.
Check the bridge length too. Bridge length changes where your hitch or device rides and how the saddle feels when you sit back, so replace it with the part Weaver specifies for the Cougar.

Fit the bridge exactly as Weaver's instructions show, with the correct routing through the saddle's attachment points and no twists. If you are unsure, have a competent person check it before you load it. The bridge is life-support equipment and must meet ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's requirements.

Inspect it before every climb. Retire the bridge if you find cuts, fuzzing that exposes inner fibers, glazing from heat, stiff or discolored areas, or damaged stitching. Many climbers also date-mark their bridges so they know how long each one has been in service.

faq.q: How often should I replace a saddle bridge?
faq.a: There is no fixed interval. Replace it whenever inspection shows wear or damage, and follow Weaver's retirement guidance.

faq.q: Can I use a rope bridge on a Cougar instead?
faq.a: Only if Weaver approves that configuration for your saddle. Do not modify a saddle beyond what the manufacturer allows.

name: Weaver Deluxe Work Suspenders with Hydration Pack
title: Weaver Deluxe Work Suspenders with Hydration Pack
h1: Weaver Deluxe Work Suspenders with Hydration Pack
meta: Weaver work suspenders with hydration pack take saddle weight off your hips and keep water on your back. Fit tips, what they are not for, and care.
tagline: Padded saddle suspenders with a built-in water bladder for long, hot climbs.
summary: Weaver work suspenders with hydration pack clip to your climbing saddle to share the weight of a loaded saddle across your shoulders, and carry a water bladder on your back so you can drink without coming down. They are a comfort item for long days aloft, not fall protection.
highlights: Shifts saddle and gear weight onto the shoulders
Hydration bladder carried on the back
Drink in the tree without descending
Padded shoulder straps
Not a chest harness or fall-arrest device
specs: Comfort and hydration, not life support

p: A saddle loaded with a top-handle saw, handsaw, carabiners, lanyard, and rope hangs on your hips all day. Suspenders spread some of that weight onto your shoulders and keep the saddle from sliding down when you are on the ground between climbs. The hydration pack solves the other problem of summer work: you can drink while you are still tied in instead of waiting until you descend.
They are especially useful on long pruning days and big removals where you are up for hours at a time. Browse more shoulder harnesses and saddle add-ons in our saddle parts and shoulder harnesses.

These suspenders are not fall protection and not a chest harness. Never clip a lanyard, rope, or rigging to them. Your climbing system stays attached to the saddle's rated attachment points, as ANSI Z133 and the saddle maker require.

Adjust the straps so the saddle sits where it is designed to, not pulled up into your waist. Rinse the bladder after each use and let it dry open to keep it clean, and check the clips and webbing for wear along with the rest of your kit.
If you climb in heat, drink early and often. Heat illness creeps up on climbers who wait until lunch to rehydrate, and a crew member who is dizzy aloft is a rescue waiting to happen.

faq.q: Will these suspenders fit any saddle?
faq.a: They are designed to clip to a climbing saddle's waist belt. Check that the attachment works with your saddle before relying on them for daily use.

faq.q: Can the suspenders work as a chest harness?
faq.a: No. They are a comfort item only and must not be used for fall arrest or any life-support connection.

name: Weaver Wideback Saddle
title: Weaver Wideback Saddle: Wide-Support Climbing Saddle
meta: The Weaver Wideback saddle is a traditional tree climbing saddle with a wide back for support. Who it suits, how to fit it, and what to inspect each day.
tagline: A traditional wide-back climbing saddle for climbers who want simple, solid support.
summary: The Weaver Wideback saddle is a traditional American-style tree climbing saddle with a wide back section that spreads your weight when you sit back in the work position. It suits climbers who like a straightforward, durable saddle without a lot of adjustment.
highlights: Wide back section spreads load in the work position
Traditional tree climbing saddle layout
Side D-rings for a lanyard or flipline
Simple, durable design
Inspect before every climb

p: Many climbers learned on a saddle like this one: a wide padded back, a front attachment, and D-rings on each side for a flipline. When you lean back to make a cut or hold position on a spar, the wide back carries the load across your lower back instead of a narrow strap.
It is a sensible choice for crews that want a no-nonsense saddle for removals, spur work, and general climbing. Compare it with Weaver's other models in our Weaver saddles section.

The trade-off for that simplicity is less adjustability than some modern European-style saddles, and fewer attachment points for SRS setups. If most of your work is spur removals and traditional doubled-rope climbing, that may not matter. If you climb SRS every day, compare the options before you buy.

Size and fit the saddle following Weaver's chart and instructions. It should sit snug on your hips without riding up, and the leg straps should not pinch. Climb only in a saddle that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's requirements, and get proper training before using any climbing system.

Inspect the saddle before each climb. Check the webbing and leather for cuts and wear, the stitching at every load point, and the D-rings and buckles for cracks, corrosion, or distortion. Retire it if anything is in doubt.

faq.q: Is the Wideback good for spur work?
faq.a: Yes. The wide back and side D-rings make it comfortable for leaning into a flipline on removals.

faq.q: How do I pick the right size?
faq.a: Use Weaver's size chart, measured over the clothes you climb in, and try it on if you can.

name: Weaver WLC-530 Climbing Saddle
title: Weaver WLC-530 Climbing Saddle
meta: The Weaver WLC-530 climbing saddle for daily tree work. Who it suits, how it compares to Weaver's other saddles, fitting advice, and daily inspection points.
tagline: A Weaver climbing saddle built for everyday tree work.
summary: The Weaver WLC-530 climbing saddle is one of Weaver Leather's tree climbing saddles, built for working climbers who want a padded, durable saddle for daily pruning and removals. Check the current Weaver spec sheet for exact sizing and attachment details before you buy.
highlights: Weaver tree climbing saddle for daily work
Padded for comfort in the work position
Side D-rings for lanyard and flipline
Durable construction for removal work

p: Weaver's WLC saddles cover a range from basic to fully featured. The WLC-530 is aimed at the climber who works aloft most days and wants a padded saddle that holds up to spurs, bark, and grit. Side D-rings take a flipline or lanyard for positioning, and the padding helps when you sit back to make cuts.
If you are choosing between models, compare attachment points, padding, and adjustability with the other options in our Weaver saddles section, and pick the one that suits how you climb.

Saddle choice is personal. Weight, padding, and where the attachment points sit all change how a saddle feels after six hours aloft. If you can, try the WLC-530 on and hang in it before committing, and think about whether you climb mostly on spurs or mostly pruning on rope.

Fit the saddle using Weaver's sizing guidance. It should be snug on the hips with the leg loops adjusted so you hang level. Use only a saddle that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's requirements, and make sure you are trained in the climbing system you plan to use.
Inspect before every climb: webbing, leather, stitching, buckles, and D-rings. Look for cuts, abrasion, heat damage, corrosion, and cracks. Retire the saddle if anything fails inspection.

faq.q: Can I use the WLC-530 for SRS?
faq.a: Check Weaver's instructions for the approved attachment points and configurations before setting it up for any climbing system.

faq.q: What should I check before each climb?
faq.a: Webbing, leather, stitching, buckles, and D-rings. Retire the saddle if you find cuts, cracks, heat damage, or distortion.

name: Weaver WLC-560 Saddle with 2 Floating D-Rings
title: Weaver WLC-560 Saddle with 2 Floating D-Rings
h1: Weaver WLC-560 Saddle with 2 Floating D-Rings
meta: The Weaver WLC-560 saddle with two floating D-rings for positioning and spur work. Why floating rings help, how to fit the saddle, and daily inspection points.
tagline: A Weaver climbing saddle with two floating D-rings for flexible positioning.
summary: The Weaver WLC-560 saddle is a tree climbing saddle fitted with two floating D-rings, which slide to follow your lanyard or flipline as you move around the stem. It suits climbers doing a lot of spur work and positioning on removals.
highlights: Two floating D-rings that move with your lanyard
Suited to spur work and removals
Padded for time in the work position
Weaver Leather construction

p: Fixed side D-rings pull your flipline from one spot, so the saddle twists when you lean around the trunk. Floating D-rings slide along the saddle, letting the lanyard load stay centered as you move and cut. On a long spar or a removal where you are constantly repositioning, that makes the saddle feel steadier and less tiring.
The WLC-560 pairs those rings with a padded body for days spent on spurs. Compare it with the WLC-530 and the Wideback in our Weaver saddles section.

Fit the saddle using Weaver's sizing and adjustment guidance so it sits snug on the hips. Use only a saddle that meets ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's requirements, attach your climbing system only where Weaver allows, and get trained before you climb.

Inspect before every climb. Check that the floating D-rings move freely and show no cracks, wear grooves, or distortion, and look over the webbing, leather, and stitching for cuts, abrasion, or heat damage. Retire the saddle if anything is in doubt.
Floating rings wear where they slide, so look closely at the contact points on the rings and the saddle. Grooves, burrs, or sharp edges are reasons to take the saddle out of service.

faq.q: What is a floating D-ring?
faq.a: A D-ring mounted so it can slide along the saddle, letting your lanyard or flipline pull from the best angle as you move.

faq.q: Is the WLC-560 a good saddle for removals?
faq.a: Yes. The floating D-rings make it well suited to spur work and frequent repositioning on removals.

name: Tree Hog Aluminum Climbers with L-Pads
title: Tree Hog Aluminum Climbers with L-Pads
h1: Tree Hog Aluminum Climbers with L-Pads
meta: Tree Hog aluminum climbers with L-pads for removal work. Why aluminum spurs save your legs, how L-pads spread the load, and what to check on gaffs and straps.
tagline: Lightweight aluminum tree spurs with L-shaped pads for removal climbers.
summary: Tree Hog aluminum climbers with L-pads are lightweight tree spurs built for removal work, with L-shaped pads that wrap the calf to spread the load. Aluminum shanks cut weight on every step compared with steel, which adds up over a day on a big spar.
highlights: Aluminum shanks for lighter legs on long climbs
L-shaped pads spread pressure across the calf
Tree gaffs for bark, not pole gaffs
For removals only, never for pruning
Inspect gaffs and straps before each climb

p: Every step up a spar lifts the weight of your spurs. Aluminum shanks are noticeably lighter than steel, and on a long removal or a day of back-to-back takedowns that difference shows up in your knees and hips. The L-shaped pads cup the calf so the load is spread instead of concentrated on a narrow strap, which helps on tall climbs.
Spurs are for removals and emergency rescue only. Gaffing a tree you are pruning wounds it for no reason. Compare other lightweight options in our aluminum spurs section.
Aluminum spurs also suit climbers who need to keep weight down on long climbs or late in the day when legs are tired, and they are easier to carry up and down hillsides to the work site.

Set the shank length so the stirrup sits under your arch and the top of the shank sits just below the knee without digging in. Keep the gaffs sharp and correctly shaped, following the maker's sharpening guidance; a dull or badly filed gaff is what causes cut-outs. Use gaff guards whenever the spurs are off your legs.

Before each climb, check gaffs for looseness, cracks, or wear below the limit, and look over straps and pads for cuts and worn buckles. Always climb on spurs with a flipline or lanyard in place, follow ANSI Z133, and get trained before you try spur work.

faq.q: Can I use these spurs to prune a tree?
faq.a: No. Spurs damage living trees and should only be used on removals or for emergency access.

faq.q: Are aluminum spurs as strong as steel?
faq.a: They are designed for climbing loads. The trade-off is weight against long-term durability, so inspect the shanks and gaffs carefully.

name: Tree Hog Aluminum Climbers with Soft Cushion Pads
title: Tree Hog Aluminum Climbers with Soft Cushion Pads
h1: Tree Hog Aluminum Climbers with Soft Cushion Pads
meta: Tree Hog aluminum climbers with soft cushion pads for comfortable removal work. How cushion pads differ from L-pads, fitting the shanks, and gaff inspection.
tagline: Lightweight aluminum spurs with soft cushion pads for long removal days.
summary: Tree Hog aluminum climbers with soft cushion pads pair light aluminum shanks with soft padded calf pads for climbers who want comfort on long removals. The cushioning helps on all-day spar work, while the aluminum keeps weight down.
highlights: Aluminum shanks keep weight down
Soft cushion pads for comfort on long climbs
Built for removal work
Use gaff guards whenever spurs are off your legs

p: Spur pads are mostly about how pressure lands on your calf. Soft cushion pads put a thick layer of padding between the shank and your leg, which many climbers prefer for long days on the spurs. L-pads wrap further around the calf for more lateral support. Both do the same job; it comes down to what feels right on your legs.
Spurs are for removals only. Gaff wounds on a tree you are keeping are an open door for decay. See the other options in our aluminum spurs section.

Soft cushion pads are also a good choice for climbers with sensitive shins or those coming back from leg strain. Try the fit with the boots you actually climb in, since boot height changes where the pad rides on the calf.

Adjust shank length so the top sits just below the knee and the stirrup is under your arch. Keep gaffs sharp and correctly profiled following the maker's guidance, and replace them when they wear past the limit. Dull gaffs cause cut-outs.

Inspect before every climb: gaff tightness and condition, shank cracks, strap and buckle wear, and pad attachment. Always climb on spurs with a flipline or lanyard, follow ANSI Z133, and get trained in spur work before you rely on it.

faq.q: Can I swap these pads for L-pads later?
faq.a: Often yes, but confirm the replacement pads are made to fit your Tree Hog shanks.

faq.q: How do I know when gaffs are worn out?
faq.a: Follow the maker's minimum length and shape guidance. A gaff that is too short, cracked, or loose must be replaced.

name: Weaver L-Shaped Climber Pads
title: Weaver L-Shaped Climber Pads for Tree Spurs
meta: Weaver L-shaped climber pads spread spur pressure across the calf for comfort on removals. How they fit, when to replace worn pads, and what to check each day.
tagline: L-shaped calf pads that make tree spurs more comfortable on long climbs.
summary: Weaver L-shaped climber pads replace worn or uncomfortable pads on tree spurs, wrapping the calf in an L-shape to spread pressure from the shank. A good set of pads is often the cheapest way to make your spurs feel better on long removals.
highlights: L-shape wraps the calf to spread pressure
Replaces worn or flattened spur pads
Makes long spar climbs more comfortable
Check compatibility with your spurs

p: When you stand in your spurs, the shank pushes against your calf with every step. Thin or flattened pads let that pressure land in one spot, and after a few hours it hurts. L-shaped pads wrap around the calf so the load is spread across a wider area, which makes a long removal noticeably easier.
They are a straightforward upgrade for older spurs or a replacement when the original pads have packed down. Browse other options in our climber pads section.

Pads are also a wear item. Sap, sweat, and rain break down the padding and covers over time, and a pad that has gone hard or flat no longer protects your leg. If your spurs fit well but hurt, the pads are the first thing to look at before you blame the shanks or straps.
Check that the pads suit your spur model and strap layout before ordering. Fit them so the shank sits centered on the pad and the upper strap holds everything snug without cutting into the leg.

Clean off sap and mud after use and let the pads dry away from direct heat. Inspect the pads, straps, and buckles each time you inspect the gaffs. Spur work should always be done with a flipline or lanyard, under ANSI Z133, by a trained climber.

faq.q: Will Weaver L-pads fit other brands of spurs?
faq.a: Many spurs share a similar layout, but confirm fit with your spur model before relying on them.

faq.q: How long do climber pads last?
faq.a: It depends on use. Replace them when the padding flattens, the cover tears, or the attachment points wear.

name: Buckingham Dowel and Screw Style Replacement Gaff Screws
title: Buckingham Replacement Gaff Screws
h1: Buckingham Replacement Gaff Screws, Dowel and Screw Style
meta: Buckingham replacement gaff screws for dowel and screw style spur gaffs. Why a loose gaff is dangerous, how to check the screw, and when to replace it.
tagline: Replacement screws that hold Buckingham dowel and screw style gaffs on the shank.
summary: These Buckingham replacement gaff screws hold dowel and screw style gaffs on Buckingham climbing spurs. A worn or stripped screw lets a gaff loosen, so having the correct replacement on hand is part of keeping spurs safe.
highlights: Replacement screw for dowel and screw style gaffs
Keeps gaffs tight on the shank
Cheap insurance against a loose gaff
Use the correct Buckingham part
specs: Buckingham dowel and screw style gaffs

p: On a dowel and screw style spur, the gaff is located by a dowel and held tight by a screw. If that screw strips, stretches, or backs out, the gaff can move under load. A gaff that rocks or shifts on the shank is a serious problem and the spurs should not be climbed on until it is fixed.
Keep a couple of Buckingham gaff screws with your spare gaffs so a worn one can be replaced at the shop rather than ignored. More parts are in our replacement gaffs and parts section.

Gaff screws also get replaced whenever you change gaffs. Reusing a worn screw on a fresh gaff is false economy. Check the threads in the shank too; damaged threads in the spur itself mean the spur needs attention from someone qualified before it goes back in service.

Use only the correct Buckingham part for your spurs and follow Buckingham's instructions for installation, including tightening and any thread-locking guidance. Do not substitute a hardware-store screw.

Before every climb, check that each gaff is tight with no play, the screw head is undamaged, and the gaff itself is sharp, uncracked, and within its wear limit. Spur work belongs to trained climbers working under ANSI Z133, always with a flipline or lanyard in place.

faq.q: Can I use a regular screw instead?
faq.a: No. Use the correct Buckingham part. The wrong screw may not hold the gaff securely.

faq.q: How do I know if a gaff screw needs replacing?
faq.a: Replace it if the threads are damaged, the head is chewed up, or the gaff will not stay tight.

name: Buckingham Magnetic Gaff Cover
title: Buckingham Magnetic Gaff Cover for Climbing Spurs
meta: The Buckingham magnetic gaff cover protects spur gaffs and the people around them. Why gaff guards matter, how a magnetic cover works, and daily care tips.
tagline: A magnetic cover that guards spur gaffs between climbs.
summary: The Buckingham magnetic gaff cover slips over a spur gaff and holds in place with a magnet, protecting the point and anyone handling the spurs. It goes on and off quickly, which makes it more likely to actually get used between climbs.
highlights: Holds on the gaff with a magnet
Quick on and off between climbs
Protects the sharpened point
Protects hands, bags, and truck seats

p: A sharp gaff is what keeps you in the tree, and it is also what cuts hands, tears gear bags, and punctures truck seats. Every time the spurs come off your legs, the gaffs should be covered. A dull or chipped gaff from rattling around the truck bed is a gaff that can cut out.
A magnetic cover is quick to put on, so it gets used. Find other guards and spur parts in our replacement gaffs and parts section.

Covers also protect the gaffs from each other. Spurs packed in a bag together will knock their points against the opposite shank every time the truck hits a pothole. A quick magnetic cover on each gaff stops that and saves a lot of time at the sharpening stone. Keep a spare cover in the truck, since they tend to get left on stumps.

Check that the cover suits your gaff style and length. Make sure the steel gaff seats fully in the cover before you pack the spurs away. Magnetic retention works on steel; confirm it holds well on your gaffs.

Keep the covers clean of sap and grit, which can dull the point. Replace a cover that is cracked or no longer holds. Inspect gaffs for sharpness, cracks, and tightness before every climb, and do spur work only with training and under ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Does the magnetic gaff cover fit every spur?
faq.a: Check it against your gaff style and length. Gaff shapes vary between makers and models.

faq.q: Should I climb with gaff covers on?
faq.a: No. Remove the covers before climbing and put them back on as soon as the spurs come off.

name: Buckingham Replacement Gaffs (Dowel Style)
title: Buckingham Replacement Gaffs, Dowel Style
meta: Buckingham replacement gaffs in dowel style for Buckingham climbing spurs. When to replace a gaff, sharpening basics, and what to check before every climb.
tagline: Dowel style replacement gaffs to keep Buckingham spurs biting.
summary: These Buckingham replacement gaffs fit Buckingham spurs that use the dowel style attachment. Gaffs wear down with sharpening and use, and swapping them is how you keep a good set of spurs biting cleanly.
highlights: Dowel style attachment for Buckingham spurs
Restores bite on worn spurs
Tree gaff profile for bark
Replace when worn past the limit
specs: Buckingham spurs with dowel style gaffs

p: Each time a gaff is sharpened, a little metal comes off. Eventually it is too short to reach through bark into solid wood, and that is when cut-outs happen. Replace gaffs when they are below the maker's minimum length, cracked, bent, or will not hold a proper edge and shape.
Check your spurs are dowel style before ordering; Buckingham has used more than one attachment design. Screws, guards, and straps are in our replacement gaffs and parts section.

Look at both gaffs side by side when you inspect. If one is noticeably shorter or a different shape, the spurs will bite unevenly and feel unsteady. Replacing both at the same time keeps them matched and is the usual practice for working climbers.

Install gaffs following Buckingham's instructions using the correct screws, and make sure they seat fully with no play. Sharpen only the way the maker recommends, keeping the original profile. Grinding the wrong faces or overheating the steel changes how the gaff bites.
Inspect gaffs before every climb and keep them covered when off your legs. Spur work should only be done by trained climbers on removals, with a flipline in place, under ANSI Z133.
Keep the old gaffs out of the parts bin so nobody reinstalls them by mistake.

faq.q: Are these gaffs sold as a pair?
faq.a: Pack quantity varies by listing. Check the product details when you buy.

faq.q: How should I sharpen tree gaffs?
faq.a: Follow Buckingham's sharpening guidance and keep the factory profile. Do not file the inside face to a needle point.

name: Weaver Bungee Gaff Guards
title: Weaver Bungee Gaff Guards for Climbing Spurs
meta: Weaver bungee gaff guards cover sharp spur gaffs between climbs and hold with an elastic cord. Why gaff guards matter, fitting tips, and when to replace them.
tagline: Gaff guards with bungee retention to protect spurs between climbs.
summary: Weaver bungee gaff guards cover your spur gaffs and hold in place with an elastic bungee cord around the shank. They keep the points sharp and keep everyone around the spurs from getting cut.
highlights: Bungee cord holds the guard on the shank
Protects gaff points in the truck
Protects hands, bags, and seats
Inexpensive spur care item

body.h: Keep gaffs sharp and people safe
p: A gaff knocks its point off fast if it rattles around a truck box with saws and wedges. A dull gaff skates on bark and leads to cut-outs. Guards protect the point between climbs and keep the gaff from slicing a gear bag or a hand reaching into one.
The bungee keeps the guard on without fiddly buckles. Other guards and spur parts are in our replacement gaffs and parts section.

Guards also stop gaffs from wearing against each other and against the shanks when spurs are packed together in a bag. Every chip off the point is metal you will have to file away to get the shape back, which shortens the life of the gaff.
Seat the gaff fully in the guard and stretch the bungee around the shank so it cannot slip off. Check that the guard suits your gaff length and style.
Replace the guard when the bungee loses its stretch or the guard is cut through. Remove guards before climbing, inspect gaffs before every climb, and follow ANSI Z133 for spur work.
Make putting guards on part of the routine: spurs off, guards on, then they go into the bag. A spare pair in the truck covers the ones that inevitably go missing at the bottom of a tree.

faq.q: Bungee or velcro gaff guards?
faq.a: Bungee guards are fast to put on; velcro guards wrap snug and adjust. Both protect the point.

faq.q: Do these fit pole gaffs?
faq.a: Check the guard size against your gaffs. Tree and pole gaffs differ in length and shape.

name: Weaver Velcro Gaff Guards
title: Weaver Velcro Gaff Guards for Climbing Spurs
meta: Weaver velcro gaff guards wrap and fasten over spur gaffs to protect the points and your hands. Why to use gaff guards, fitting tips, and when to replace them.
tagline: Hook-and-loop gaff guards that wrap snug over spur gaffs.
summary: Weaver velcro gaff guards wrap over your spur gaffs and close with hook-and-loop, giving a snug, adjustable fit. They protect the points from damage and protect you and your gear from the points.
highlights: Hook-and-loop closure for a snug fit
Protects gaff points between climbs
Prevents cuts to hands and gear
Simple and inexpensive

body.h: Why every set of spurs needs guards
p: Sharp gaffs are a hazard off the tree. They cut hands reaching into a bag, tear rope, and dull themselves on metal tools. Covering them every time the spurs come off is a habit worth building, and it keeps the points in shape for the next removal.
Velcro guards wrap snug and adjust to the gaff. See other guards and parts in our replacement gaffs and parts section.

A spare set of gaff guards costs less than one replacement gaff, and much less than a cut hand. Get the crew in the habit of covering gaffs the moment spurs come off, before they go into a bag or behind the truck seat. Chipped points also take longer to sharpen and shorten the life of the gaff.
Wrap the guard fully over the gaff and press the closure firmly. Keep the hook-and-loop clean of bark, sawdust, and sap so it keeps holding.
Replace guards that no longer close properly or are cut through. Remove guards before climbing, inspect gaffs before every climb, and follow ANSI Z133 for spur work.
If you also carry bungee guards, the two styles can be mixed; what matters is that every gaff is covered whenever the spurs are off.

faq.q: Will velcro guards stay on in the truck?
faq.a: Yes, if the closure is clean and pressed firmly. Replace them once the hook-and-loop wears out.

faq.q: Should I use guards on gaffs in storage?
faq.a: Yes. Keep gaffs covered any time the spurs are off your legs.

name: Buckingham Universal Lower Straps
title: Buckingham Universal Lower Straps for Climbing Spurs
meta: Buckingham universal lower straps hold climbing spurs at the ankle and boot. When to replace worn spur straps, how to fit them, and what to check each day.
tagline: Replacement lower straps that hold spurs snug at the ankle.
summary: Buckingham universal lower straps replace the ankle straps on climbing spurs, holding the stirrup snug against your boot. A worn lower strap lets the spur shift on every step, so replacing it is basic spur maintenance.
highlights: Replacement lower (ankle) straps for spurs
Universal fit for many spur models
Holds the stirrup snug to the boot
Replace when cut, cracked, or stretched

p: The lower strap wraps over your boot and holds the spur stirrup in place under your arch. If it is stretched, cracked, or loose, the spur rolls and shifts as you step in, which costs energy and makes cut-outs more likely. Lower straps also take a beating from brush, mud, and saw chips, so they wear out well before the shank does.
Universal straps suit many spur models, but check the strap layout on your spurs before ordering. Gaffs and other spur parts are in our replacement gaffs and parts section.
Replace both lower straps at the same time, even if only one looks bad. Matched straps wear the same way and make it easier to set both spurs to the same tension so they feel even on your legs.
Thread the strap so it crosses the boot as the spur maker intends and cinch it snug without cutting off circulation. Wear sturdy boots with a defined heel and a stiff shank for spur work.

Inspect the straps and buckles each time you check the gaffs. Replace straps that are cut, cracked, dried out, or have elongated holes. Spur work belongs to trained climbers on removals, with a flipline or lanyard in place, under ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Do universal lower straps fit every spur?
faq.a: They suit many common spurs. Compare the strap width and layout with your spurs before ordering.

faq.q: How tight should lower straps be?
faq.a: Snug enough that the stirrup does not shift under the boot, but not so tight it cuts circulation.

name: Weaver 26" Leather Lower Straps
title: Weaver Leather Lower Straps for Spurs, 26 Inch
meta: Weaver leather lower straps, 26 inch, for climbing spurs. How lower straps hold the stirrup, caring for leather so it lasts, and when to replace a worn strap.
tagline: Leather 26 inch lower straps for keeping climbing spurs snug at the boot.
summary: Weaver leather lower straps are 26 inch replacement ankle straps for climbing spurs. Leather molds to the boot over time and holds the stirrup firmly, and with a little care it lasts a long time.
highlights: 26 inch leather lower straps
Holds the spur stirrup snug to the boot
Leather conforms to the boot with use
Replace when cracked or stretched

p: Leather has been the traditional choice for spur straps for good reason. It holds a buckle well, molds to the shape of your boot over time, and stays put once it is broken in. A lower strap that holds the stirrup snug under your arch keeps the spur from rolling as you step up a spar.
Check that 26 inch straps suit your spurs and boots. More spur straps, gaffs, and guards are in our replacement gaffs and parts section.

New leather is stiff for the first few days on the spurs. Expect to re-tighten the straps a few times while they break in, and check them again halfway through your first climbs. Once broken in, they hold their shape and settle into the curve of your boot.

Leather lasts when it is cared for. Wipe off mud and sap, let it dry slowly away from heat, and condition it so it does not dry out and crack. Leather that stays wet or is baked dry fails much sooner.

Inspect straps before every climb. Replace any that are cracked, cut, stretched at the holes, or have damaged buckles. Do spur work only on removals, with training, a flipline in place, and under ANSI Z133.
Store spurs and straps somewhere dry and ventilated, not sealed in a plastic bin with damp gear.

faq.q: Leather or webbing straps?
faq.a: Leather molds to the boot and lasts with care. Webbing handles water better and needs less upkeep.

faq.q: How do I care for leather spur straps?
faq.a: Clean, dry slowly, and condition them. Avoid leaving them wet or near direct heat.

name: Weaver Brahma 26" Upper Climber Straps
title: Weaver Brahma Upper Climber Straps, 26 Inch
meta: Weaver Brahma upper climber straps in 26 inch length hold the top of your spurs snug below the knee. Fitting tips, care, and when to replace worn straps.
tagline: 26 inch upper straps that hold spur shanks snug below the knee.
summary: Weaver Brahma upper climber straps are 26 inch replacement straps that wrap the calf just below the knee and hold the top of the spur shank in place. A solid upper strap keeps the shank from wandering when you load your spurs.
highlights: 26 inch upper (calf) straps
Holds the top of the shank in place
Replacement for worn upper straps
Check fit with your spurs and pads

p: The upper strap wraps around your calf just below the knee and holds the shank and pad tight to your leg. When it is worn or loose, the top of the spur moves around with each step, and the pad rubs instead of supporting. A good upper strap is a large part of what makes spurs feel stable on a spar.
Measure your current straps and confirm 26 inch fits your calf and pads. Lower straps, gaffs, and guards are in our replacement gaffs and parts section.
Replace both upper straps together so they wear evenly and feel the same on each leg. If your current straps have stretched to the last hole, that is a clear sign it is time.
Cinch the upper strap snug but not so tight it bites into the back of the knee or restricts circulation. Make sure it sits below the knee joint so it does not limit bending.

Inspect straps and buckles each time you inspect your gaffs. Replace straps that are cut, cracked, stretched at the holes, or have bent buckles. Spur work is for removals only, by trained climbers, with a flipline in place and following ANSI Z133.
Keep a spare set in the truck for the day one gets cut.

faq.q: Do Brahma upper straps fit any spur?
faq.a: They suit many spurs with standard strap slots. Compare widths and layout with your spurs before ordering.

faq.q: Where should the upper strap sit?
faq.a: Just below the knee, snug enough to hold the shank without limiting how the knee bends.

name: Weaver Brahma Webb Lower Climber Straps
keyword: weaver brahma webb lower climber straps
title: Weaver Brahma Webb Lower Climber Straps
h1: Weaver Brahma Webb Lower Climber Straps
meta: Weaver Brahma Webb lower climber straps hold spur stirrups snug to the boot with low-upkeep webbing. Fitting tips, care, and when to replace lower spur straps.
tagline: Webbing lower straps for spurs that handle wet days without much care.
summary: Weaver Brahma Webb lower climber straps are webbing replacement ankle straps for climbing spurs. Webbing shrugs off rain and mud better than leather and needs less upkeep, while still holding the stirrup snug to your boot.
highlights: Webbing lower (ankle) straps
Handles wet conditions with little upkeep
Holds the stirrup snug under the arch
Replacement for worn lower straps

p: Lower straps live in the wettest, dirtiest spot on your spurs: down at the boot, in mud, wet grass, and sawdust. Webbing does not need conditioning, dries quickly, and does not crack the way neglected leather can. For crews working in wet climates or climbers who do not want to baby their gear, webbing is the practical choice.
Confirm the strap suits your spur layout before ordering. Upper straps, gaffs, and guards are in our replacement gaffs and parts section.

Webbing straps are also a good match for climbers who work storm cleanups and wet-season removals, when gear rarely gets a chance to dry out between jobs. Replace both lower straps at once so they cinch the same on each leg, and keep a spare set in the truck for when one gets cut by a gaff or a chain.
Route the strap across the boot as your spur maker intends and cinch it so the stirrup cannot shift. Wear boots with a solid heel and shank for spur work.

Inspect the webbing and buckles before every climb. Replace straps that are cut, frayed, melted, or have damaged hardware. Spur work belongs on removals, done by trained climbers with a flipline in place, following ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Will webbing straps stretch when wet?
faq.a: Webbing holds up well in wet conditions. Re-check tightness during the day either way.

faq.q: How do I clean webbing spur straps?
faq.a: Rinse off mud and sap with water and mild soap and let them air dry.

name: Weaver 16 oz Throw Weight and Line Kit
keyword: weaver throw weight and line kit
title: Weaver Throw Weight and Line Kit, 16 oz
h1: Weaver Throw Weight and Line Kit (16 oz)
meta: The Weaver throw weight and line kit with a 16 oz bag sets climbing lines and rigging points. When to use a heavier bag, throwing tips, and keeping line tidy.
tagline: A 16 oz throw bag and line for setting climbing lines through thick canopy.
summary: The Weaver throw weight and line kit pairs a 16 oz throw weight with throw line, giving you what you need to set a climbing line or rigging point from the ground. The heavier bag is easier to drive through dense canopy and bring back down on the far side.
highlights: 16 oz throw weight
Throw line included
Heavier bag drives through dense canopy
Sets climbing lines and rigging points from the ground

body.h: When a 16 oz bag makes sense
p: Throw bag weight is a trade-off. Lighter bags fly higher and are easier to throw; heavier bags push through leaves and small twigs and pull line back down over a high, rough crotch. A 16 oz bag is the choice for big trees, dense crowns, and limbs with lots of bark friction where a light bag just hangs up.
Many climbers carry two weights and swap as needed. See other bags and lines in our throw line section.
A heavy bag is also handy for isolating a specific union. Once the line is over, the extra weight helps you lower the bag smoothly and control where it comes down.

Lay out or bag the line so it pays out cleanly, check the drop zone is clear of people, traffic, and power lines, and throw underhand with a smooth swing. Keep your eyes on the bag in case it comes back fast. Never throw anywhere near energized conductors; ANSI Z133 sets minimum approach distances.

Store the line in a cube or bag so it is ready to go next time. Check it for nicks and fused spots, and replace it when it starts to break. Throw line is for setting lines only, never for climbing or rigging loads.

faq.q: Is 16 oz too heavy for beginners?
faq.a: It takes more effort to throw high, but it is easier to get back down through the canopy. Many people start with a mid-weight bag.

faq.q: Can I climb on throw line?
faq.a: No. Throw line is only for pulling a climbing or rigging line into place.

name: FTC 1.6 mm Stiffline
title: FTC Stiffline 1.6 mm Throw Line
meta: FTC Stiffline is a 1.6 mm stiff throw line that resists tangles and slides over bark. Who it suits, how to store it, and why throw line is never for climbing.
tagline: A thin, stiff throw line that runs clean and resists tangling.
summary: FTC Stiffline is a 1.6 mm throw line with a stiff construction that resists tangles and slides over bark and through crotches with little drag. The stiffness helps the line feed cleanly from a cube and keeps it from snagging on twigs as you pull it through.
highlights: 1.6 mm diameter
Stiff construction resists tangles
Low friction over bark
For setting lines only, not for climbing

body.h: Why a stiff throw line helps
p: Soft throw line has a habit of knotting into itself the moment you look away. A stiffer line resists that, pays out more cleanly from a cube or bag, and is less likely to wrap around twigs when you are pulling it back down. The thin diameter keeps drag low so a light throw weight can still get height.
Pair it with a throw weight that suits your trees. Other lines and kits are in our throw line section.

Stiff line is also easier to manipulate once it is in the tree. When you need to move it to a different union, flipping or snapping the line along the limb works better with a line that holds its shape. Many climbers find that alone saves several re-throws on a busy day.

Feed the line into a storage cube or bag after each use rather than coiling it. Check the drop zone is clear before each throw, and keep throws well away from power lines in line with ANSI Z133 approach distances.

Inspect the line for flat spots, glazing, and nicks, and cut out damage or replace it. Throw line is only for pulling a climbing line or rigging line into place. Never climb on it or use it to hold a load.

faq.q: What throw weight works with 1.6 mm line?
faq.a: It works with common throw weights. Pick the bag weight to suit how high and how dense the canopy is.

faq.q: Does Stiffline need a special storage cube?
faq.a: Any throw line cube or bag works. Stuff the line loosely so it pays out without tangling.

name: Petzl Airline Throwline
title: Petzl Airline Throwline for Arborists
meta: Petzl Airline is a thin, low-friction throwline for setting climbing and rigging lines. How it handles in the canopy, storage, and why it is never for climbing.
tagline: A thin, slick throwline from Petzl for setting climbing lines.
summary: Petzl Airline is a thin, slick throwline made for arborists to set climbing and rigging lines in the canopy. Its smooth finish lets it slide over bark and through unions with little friction, and it pairs with Petzl's Jet throw weights or any common throw bag.
highlights: Thin, low-friction throwline
Slides easily over bark and unions
Works with Petzl Jet and other throw weights
For setting lines only, not for climbing

p: A good throwline gets out of the way: it pays out without tangles, slides over bark so you can walk the line where you want it, and pulls a climbing line into place without sawing at the tree. Airline is thin and slick, which keeps friction down and lets a moderate throw bag gain height.
Pair it with a throw weight that suits the canopy and store it in a cube. Other lines and kits are in our throw line section.

Once the line is over a limb, the slick finish also helps when you need to isolate a union. You can flip the line along a branch, pull the bag up to a lower crotch, or walk it around to a better tie-in point without fighting friction. That saves throws, and saves your arm on a long day of setting lines for climbs and rigging.
Check the drop zone before every throw and keep well clear of power lines, following ANSI Z133 approach distances. Watch the bag on the way down.

Stuff the line loosely into its storage bag after each use. Inspect it for flat spots, fused areas, and abrasion, and replace it once it starts to break. Throwline is never for climbing or for holding a load.

faq.q: Can I use Airline with a non-Petzl throw bag?
faq.a: Yes. It works with common throw weights; tie it on with a secure knot.

faq.q: Why does a thin throwline help?
faq.a: Less diameter means less friction over bark and through unions, so the bag gets more height and the line is easier to pull through.

name: Weaver 12 oz Throw Weight and Line Kit
title: Weaver 12 oz Throw Weight and Line Kit
h1: Weaver 12 oz Throw Weight and Line Kit
meta: The Weaver 12 oz throw weight and line kit sets climbing lines and rigging points. Why 12 oz is a good all-round bag, throwing tips, and caring for the line.
tagline: A 12 oz throw bag and line, a good all-round choice for most trees.
summary: The Weaver 12 oz throw weight and line kit gives you a mid-weight throw bag and throw line for setting climbing lines and rigging points from the ground. A 12 oz bag is a good all-round weight: light enough to throw high, heavy enough to come back down through most canopies.
highlights: 12 oz throw weight
Throw line included
All-round weight for most trees
Sets climbing and rigging lines from the ground

body.h: Why 12 oz is a good starting weight
p: If you only carry one throw bag, a mid-weight is the sensible pick. It flies high enough for most residential and park trees, and it has enough mass to pull line back down through moderate foliage and over a rough union. Lighter bags go higher but hang up easier; heavier ones punch through but take more effort.
Climbers who work big, dense trees often add a heavier bag later. See other bags and lines in our throw line section.

For a first kit, a mid-weight bag is also forgiving while you build your technique. It does not punish a sloppy throw as much as a heavy bag, and it is easier to retrieve when the bag lands in a crotch you did not intend. Practice in an open area before throwing over a work tree.
Check the drop zone, call your throw, and keep well away from power lines according to ANSI Z133. Throw with a smooth underhand swing and watch the bag all the way down.

Store the line in a bag or cube so it pays out cleanly. Inspect it for nicks and fused spots and replace it when worn. Throw line is only for pulling up a climbing or rigging line, never for climbing or rigging loads.

faq.q: Is 12 oz good for a first throw bag?
faq.a: Yes. It is a balanced weight that suits most trees and is easy to learn on.

faq.q: How do I keep throw line from tangling?
faq.a: Stuff it loosely into a cube or bag rather than coiling it, and let it pay out from the bag when you throw.

name: Orange Laces for Scafell Lite Boots
title: Orange Replacement Laces for Scafell Lite Boots
h1: Orange Laces for Scafell Lite Boots
meta: Orange replacement laces for Scafell Lite boots from Arbortec. Why to replace worn laces before they snap, lacing tips for a snug fit, and boot care basics.
tagline: Orange replacement laces for Arbortec Scafell Lite chainsaw boots.
summary: These orange laces for Scafell Lite boots replace worn laces on Arbortec's Scafell Lite chainsaw boots. Laces wear through on hooks and eyelets long before a good boot is finished, and a fresh pair keeps the boot snug on the foot where it belongs.
highlights: Replacement laces for Scafell Lite boots
High-visibility orange
Keep a spare pair in the truck
Cheap fix that keeps boots fitting right

p: Boot laces wear at the hooks and eyelets, and in a chainsaw boot they also pick up sawdust, mud, and bar oil that grind at the fibers. A lace that snaps halfway through a climb or while you are bucking leaves the boot loose on your foot, which is exactly when ankles roll and spurs shift.
Swapping laces when they start to fuzz is cheap and quick. Keep a spare pair in the truck. More footwear is in our arborist boots section.
Orange is also easy to spot against mud.

Lace the boot firmly through the instep so your heel stays seated, and tuck or trim the ends so they cannot catch on brush, spur straps, or a chain. A well-laced boot is part of how a chainsaw boot and spurs work as designed.

Clean mud and sawdust off your boots at the end of the day and let them dry away from direct heat. Check the uppers, the cut-protection areas, and the soles for damage, and follow the boot maker's guidance on when to replace them.
Re-check your laces at lunch. Lacing loosens as boots flex and warm up, and a quick re-tie keeps your heel locked in for the afternoon climb.

faq.q: Will these laces fit other boots?
faq.a: They are sold for Scafell Lite boots. They may fit similar boots, but check the length against your current laces.

faq.q: Why orange laces?
faq.a: They match the Scafell Lite's look and are easy to spot, which helps when you are checking that your boots are laced and tucked.

name: Arbortec BreatheDry Waterproof Smock (Black, Large)
title: Arbortec BreatheDry Waterproof Smock, Black
meta: The Arbortec BreatheDry waterproof smock is a breathable pullover for wet days in the tree. Why a smock suits climbers, how to fit it, and how to care for it.
tagline: A waterproof, breathable pullover smock for climbing and groundwork in the rain.
summary: The Arbortec BreatheDry waterproof smock is a breathable pullover jacket for tree work in wet weather, shown here in black, size large. A smock has no full-length front zip, so there is less to snag and nothing to fail when you are climbing, rigging, or dragging brush in the rain.
highlights: Waterproof, breathable BreatheDry fabric
Pullover smock design with no full front zip
Less to snag on branches and gear
Black, size large

p: A full-zip jacket under a saddle is awkward: the zip bunches under the waist belt, the hem catches on hardware, and the front can work open. A smock pulls over your head, sits cleanly under the saddle, and has less to snag on branches. Breathable fabric matters too, because a fully sealed jacket soaks you in sweat by the second climb.
It works just as well on the ground for chipping, dragging brush, and running ropes in a downpour. See more jackets and layers in our sweatshirts and jackets section.
Black hides sap and bar oil better than lighter colors, but it is not high-visibility. On road jobs or busy sites, add the high-visibility garment the job requires.

Check the size against your usual layers; you want room for a fleece underneath and enough arm length to reach overhead without the hem lifting. Make sure the smock does not cover or interfere with your saddle's attachment points.

Wash it following the care label, using a cleaner suited to waterproof fabrics rather than standard detergent, and reproof it when water stops beading on the surface. Keep it away from bar oil and fuel where you can, as they can affect the coating.

faq.q: Can I wear the smock over a climbing saddle?
faq.a: Most climbers wear it under the saddle. Make sure it does not cover or interfere with your attachment points.

faq.q: How do I keep it waterproof?
faq.a: Wash with a technical fabric cleaner and reproof it when water stops beading, following the care label.

name: Arborwear Tech Double Thick Pullover Sweatshirt (Black/Safety Yellow)
keyword: arborwear tech double thick pullover sweatshirt
title: Arborwear Tech Double Thick Pullover Sweatshirt
h1: Arborwear Tech Double Thick Pullover Sweatshirt
meta: The Arborwear Tech Double Thick pullover sweatshirt in black and safety yellow. A warm, high-visibility layer for cold mornings on the ground and in the tree.
tagline: A heavy, two-tone pullover for cold days on the crew, in black and safety yellow.
summary: The Arborwear Tech Double Thick pullover sweatshirt is a heavyweight work sweatshirt built for tree crews, here in black with safety yellow. It is the layer you reach for on cold mornings, warm enough to work in and bright enough to be seen on the ground.
highlights: Heavy double-thick construction for warmth
Black and safety yellow color scheme
Pullover design with nothing to snag
Built for work, not the couch

body.h: A working layer for cold days
p: Fall cleanups and winter removals start cold. A heavy pullover keeps your core warm while you set up, run the chipper, or wait for the crane, and it holds up to brush, bark, and the rub of a saddle better than a light hoodie. The safety yellow panels add visibility for ground workers near traffic and equipment.
Layer it under a shell when it rains and peel it off once you are working hard. More layers are in our sweatshirts and jackets section.
A pullover also has no zipper to snag on bark or gear, and no open front to flap around while you work. It stays put under a saddle or a chainsaw chap harness and does not bunch the way a hoodie can.

Pick a size that lets you reach overhead and lean back in a saddle without the hem riding up. Loose cuffs and drawstrings can catch in a chipper or a rope system, so keep them tucked and never wear loose clothing near chippers or stump grinders.

A bright sweatshirt helps, but it is not a substitute for ANSI-rated high-visibility apparel where a job, road work zone, or employer requires it. Wash it per the care label to keep the colors bright.

faq.q: Is this sweatshirt a hi-vis garment?
faq.a: It adds visibility, but do not treat it as rated high-visibility apparel unless the label states a certification.

faq.q: Can I climb in it?
faq.a: Yes, as a warm layer. Keep it from interfering with your saddle and keep cuffs and hems tidy.

name: Teufelberger Arctic Climbing Fleece (Large)
title: Teufelberger Arctic Climbing Fleece, Large
meta: The Teufelberger Arctic climbing fleece is a warm mid-layer for cold-weather climbing and groundwork. Layering it under a saddle, sizing, and care basics.
tagline: A warm fleece mid-layer for climbing in the cold, in size large.
summary: The Teufelberger Arctic climbing fleece is a warm mid-layer for climbers working through cold weather, shown here in size large. Fleece stays warm when damp, breathes when you are working hard, and moves with you when you reach and lean in the saddle.
highlights: Warm fleece mid-layer
Stays warm when damp
Moves with you in the saddle
Size large

p: Climbing in winter is a balance. You are cold on the ground and on the drive in, then sweating halfway up the tree. A fleece mid-layer handles that range well: it traps warmth when you are still, breathes when you are working, and keeps insulating even if it gets damp. Put a shell over it in rain or snow and you are set for most days.
Fleece also sits well under a saddle without bunching. Find more layers in our sweatshirts and jackets section.

On the coldest days, pair the fleece with a thin base layer and a windproof shell. Three thin layers you can adjust beat one heavy coat you have to take off halfway up the tree and clip to your saddle.

Choose a size that leaves room to reach overhead and to sit back in the work position without the hem pulling out. Make sure the fleece does not cover or interfere with your saddle's attachment points.

Fleece and chainsaws do not mix well; it can snag and pill on bark, and it offers no cut protection. Wear proper chainsaw protection where required. Wash per the care label and skip fabric softener, which can reduce how well fleece breathes.

faq.q: Can I wear the fleece under a waterproof jacket?
faq.a: Yes. It works well as a mid-layer under a shell or smock.

faq.q: Does this fleece fit true to size?
faq.a: Check the maker's size chart and allow room for a base layer and movement in the saddle.

name: Arborwear Transpiration T-Shirt (Safety Yellow)
title: Arborwear Transpiration T-Shirt, Safety Yellow
meta: The Arborwear Transpiration t-shirt in safety yellow is a lightweight work tee for hot days on tree crews. Why it suits climbers, fit notes, and hi-vis caveats.
tagline: A lightweight, bright work tee for hot days in the tree and on the ground.
summary: The Arborwear Transpiration t-shirt is a lightweight work tee built for hot days, here in safety yellow. It is made to handle sweat better than a plain cotton tee, and the bright color helps ground workers and climbers stay visible on the job.
highlights: Lightweight tee for hot-weather work
Handles sweat better than plain cotton
Safety yellow color for visibility
Comfortable under a saddle

p: July removals are hard enough without a soaked cotton shirt sticking to your back. A tee made to move moisture helps keep you a little cooler and drier through a long climb or a day of feeding the chipper. The bright color helps the climber see the ground crew and the ground crew see each other near equipment and traffic.
It layers under a work shirt or sweatshirt on cooler mornings too. Browse more crew clothing in our clothing section.
Lightweight tees also dry faster when you take a break, which helps when you climb back up after lunch. Many crews buy them in bulk and wear a fresh one each day through the hottest months.
Pick a fit that does not ride up when you reach or lean back in a saddle, and that is not so loose it catches on branches. Keep any loose clothing away from chippers and stump grinders.

A safety yellow tee adds visibility but is not a substitute for ANSI-rated high-visibility apparel where the job or a road work zone requires it. Drink water, take breaks in the shade, and watch your crew for signs of heat illness on hot days.
Wash it per the care label.

faq.q: Is this t-shirt rated high-visibility apparel?
faq.a: Treat it as a bright work tee. Use certified high-visibility apparel where a job or work zone requires it.

faq.q: Does it work as a base layer in winter?
faq.a: Yes. It can be worn under a sweatshirt or fleece on cold days.

name: Fanno 13" Tri-Edge Blade
title: Fanno Tri-Edge Blade for Pole Saws, 13 Inch
meta: The Fanno tri-edge blade is a 13 inch replacement pruning saw blade for pole saws. How tri-edge teeth cut, matching the blade to your saw head, and blade care.
tagline: A 13 inch tri-edge replacement blade for pole pruning saws.
summary: The Fanno tri-edge blade is a 13 inch replacement pruning blade with tri-edge teeth that cut on the pull stroke. It is a common replacement for pole saw heads, and a fresh blade brings a tired saw back to cutting fast.
highlights: 13 inch replacement pruning blade
Tri-edge teeth cut on the pull stroke
Common pole saw replacement
Cheaper than replacing the whole head

p: Tri-edge teeth are ground on three faces, so each tooth slices fibers cleanly on the pull stroke instead of tearing them. That means faster cuts with less effort, and a cleaner pruning wound on the live limbs you are leaving. On a pole saw, where you are working overhead at arm's length, a sharp blade is the difference between three pulls and ten.
Tri-edge teeth are usually hardened and are not meant to be filed. When the blade dulls, replace it. More blades are in our blades section.

Keeping a spare blade in the truck is cheap insurance. A pole saw blade can kink if it binds in a cut, and with a spare you can swap it on site and keep the job moving instead of driving back for another saw.
Check the mounting holes and length match your saw head before ordering, and bolt the blade in with the correct hardware, snug and without play. A loose blade wanders and can bind or break.

Wipe sap off after use, keep the blade lightly oiled against rust, and cover it in transport. When pruning near power lines, only qualified line-clearance arborists should work within ANSI Z133 approach distances, using properly rated insulated tools.

faq.q: Can I sharpen a tri-edge blade?
faq.a: Tri-edge teeth are generally hardened and not meant to be filed. Replace the blade when it dulls.

faq.q: Will this blade fit my pole saw head?
faq.a: Compare length and mounting hole pattern with your current blade before ordering.

summary: The Jameson tri-cut saw blade is a 13 inch replacement pole saw blade with tri-cut teeth and a hook at the tip. The teeth cut fast on the pull stroke, and the hook helps you pull down hangers and clear small limbs without switching tools.

Tri-cut teeth for fast pull-stroke cuts
Hook at the tip for pulling hangers
Swap a dull blade, keep the saw head

p: When you are pruning with a pole saw, cut limbs often hang up in the crown. The hook at the tip of this blade lets you reach up and pull a hanger free or rake small cut pieces down without putting the saw down for another tool. The tri-cut teeth slice cleanly on the pull stroke, leaving a tidy cut on the limb you are keeping.
Tri-cut teeth are hardened and generally not filed, so replace the blade when it dulls. See other blades in our blades section.
Pull hangers with care. Stand clear of where the limb will drop and do not yank on a piece that is still holding load. A spare blade in the truck keeps you working if one kinks in a bind.
Make sure the length and mounting holes match your Jameson saw head or other compatible head. Bolt it on tight with no play.

Clean sap off, oil lightly, and keep it covered in the truck. Watch where cut limbs and hangers will fall before you pull them, and keep the ground crew clear. Near power lines, only qualified line-clearance workers may work within ANSI Z133 approach distances, using rated insulated tools.
Keep a spare blade handy.

name: Silky Gunfighter 330 mm Replacement Blade
title: Silky Gunfighter Replacement Blade, 330 mm
h1: Silky Gunfighter Replacement Blade (330 mm, Blade Only)
meta: A Silky Gunfighter replacement blade, 330 mm with taper-ground teeth. Why taper grinding cuts cleaner, how to fit it to your handle, and blade care tips.
tagline: A 330 mm taper-ground replacement blade for the Silky Gunfighter saw.
summary: This Silky Gunfighter replacement blade is a 330 mm blade with taper-ground teeth, sold as the blade only. Swapping a dull or kinked blade into your existing handle and scabbard costs much less than a new saw and brings back Silky's fast, clean cut.
highlights: 330 mm replacement blade, blade only
Taper-ground blade reduces binding
Fits the Silky Gunfighter handle
Swap in when the old blade dulls or kinks

p: A taper-ground blade is thicker along the teeth and thinner along the back. That gives it clearance in the kerf, so it binds less in green wood and pulls through with less effort. Combined with Silky's pull-stroke teeth, it leaves a smooth cut, which is what you want on the limbs you are pruning back to a collar.
Silky teeth are hardened and not meant to be filed. When the blade is dull or bent, swap it. More blades are in our blades section.

Replacing just the blade also means you keep a handle you already know and a scabbard that is already set up on your saddle. Climbers who prune every day often keep a spare blade in the truck so a kinked blade does not end the day early.
Confirm the blade is the Gunfighter 330 mm version before ordering, then fit it using Silky's instructions so the blade locks firmly in the handle with no wobble.

Wipe off sap and moisture after use, apply a light coat of oil, and keep the blade in its scabbard. Never twist or pry with the saw; that is how blades kink and snap. Keep your free hand clear of the cut line, especially when working from a saddle.

faq.q: Does this include a handle or scabbard?
faq.a: No. It is the replacement blade only, for use with your existing Gunfighter handle.

faq.q: Can I sharpen a Silky blade?
faq.a: Silky teeth are impulse-hardened and not meant to be filed. Replace the blade when it gets dull.
